question: Why does this proxy relay a forwarded upstream answer as raw bytes instead of fully decoding every record type and re-encoding a fresh response, the way 15-dns-resolver does?
answer_hinglish:
Seedha jawab: safety ke liye. Yeh proxy sirf itna hi decode karta hai jitna decision lene ke liye zaroori hai -- header, question, aur upstream answer ka name/type/class/ttl -- aur rdata ko uski rdlength se SKIP kar deta hai, kabhi interpret nahi karta. Jo bhi client ko relay hota hai woh upstream ke EXACT bytes hote hain, sirf 2-byte transaction id patched hota hai cache-hit case mein.

Reason yeh hai ki ek undecoded rdata (CNAME, NS, MX, SOA, PTR types) ke andar ek DNS-COMPRESSED name ho sakta hai, aur ek compression pointer sirf us EXACT packet ke bytes ke relative valid hota hai jisme woh likha gaya tha. Agar hum decode-reencode karte -- naya header, shayad alag question encoding -- aur us rdata ko bina samjhe copy kar dete, pointer WRONG offset point karne lagta naye packet mein. Yeh silent corruption hota, crash nahi -- aur isko pakadna crash se zyada hard hota.

15-dns-resolver yeh risk le sakta hai kyunki woh ek full resolver hai, apne clients ke liye fresh records banata hai, aur sirf un types ko decode karta hai jinke encoders bhi usne likhe hain. Yeh proxy sirf relay karta hai, isliye 'jo samajh nahi aata use touch mat karo' safest aur simplest dono hai -- aur isi wajah se A/AAAA/NS/CNAME/SOA/MX/TXT/PTR ke liye koi encoder likhne ki zaroorat nahi padti.
why_needed: Interviewer yeh test karta hai ki candidate DNS message compression ke internals samajhta hai, aur 'relay unchanged' vs 'decode and rebuild' ke correctness trade-off ko articulate kar sakta hai -- ek common senior-level DNS/network-proxy design question.
real_world_analogy: Ek sealed courier envelope ko dusre shehar forward karna bina khole -- agar andar ka content kisi doosre document ko REFER karta ho (jaise 'page 3 ka point dekho', jahan 'page 3' sirf ORIGINAL bundle mein valid hai), toh envelope khol ke content ko naye bundle mein daalna woh reference tod dega.
how_it_works: decodeResponse sirf header + questions + har answer ka name/type/class/ttl padhta hai; rdlength field se rdata ko bina parse kiye skip karta hai. Jo buffer client ko jaata hai woh forwardQuery se aaya hua EXACT upstream reply hai -- proxy.ts ka handle() sirf cache-hit path mein 2-byte id patch karta hai (patchId), aur cache.ts ka get() sirf fixed-position 4-byte TTL fields patch karta hai, kabhi rdata ya naam nahi.
in_this_project: src/wire.ts ke decodeResponse mein for loop har answer ke liye name, type, class, ttl (ttlOffset record karte hue) padhta hai, phir r.skip(rdlength, "rdata") se rdata skip karta hai bina ek byte bhi interpret kiye. src/proxy.ts ka handle() upstream se aaya replyBuf seedha return karta hai forwarded case mein -- koi re-encode nahi.
advantages: Compression-pointer corruption ka pura class of bug eliminate ho jaata hai
Bahut kam code -- A/AAAA ke bina koi RR encoder likhne ki zaroorat nahi
Upstream jo bhi bhejta hai (jaise EDNS options) wahi client tak pahunchta hai, kuch drop nahi hota
disadvantages: Proxy khud kisi bhi rdata ka content inspect nahi kar sakta (jaise CNAME target par blocklist/allowlist apply karna -- abhi dono sirf query name par match karte hain)
Agar kabhi full decode add karna ho (naya feature), yahi compression-pointer risk wapas introduce ho jaayega
common_mistakes: Yeh sochna ki 'hum TTL decode kar rahe hain toh hum pura record bhi decode kar sakte hain' -- TTL ek fixed-position integer hai, rdata nahi
Rdata ko 'parse karne ki koshish karo, fail ho toh skip karo' jaisa approach lena -- yeh silent corruption ko catch nahi karega, sirf crash ko
follow_up_questions: If you needed the allowlist/blocklist to also match CNAME targets, what new risk would full RR decoding introduce?
Why is patching a cache hit's transaction ID safe but patching rdata would not be?
What specifically makes a TTL field safe to patch in place that rdata is not?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Decode-minimal + raw relay vs full decode-reencode -- pehla approach security/correctness ko prioritize karta hai code complexity ke upar; dusra approach (15-dns-resolver jaisa) flexibility deta hai (apna format control) par har record type ka encoder sahi likhna padta hai, aur naming/compression bugs ka surface area badh jaata hai.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar kabhi accidentally rdata decode-reencode karna start kar diya jaaye (jaise naya feature add karte waqt) bina compression-pointer validity check ke, toh ek CNAME chain wala response client ko CORRUPT bytes bhej sakta hai -- client resolver parse fail karega ya wrong address resolve karega, aur yeh sirf SPECIFIC upstream responses (jinme compression use hota hai) par trigger hoga, intermittent aur debug-hard.
advanced.alternatives: Full decode-reencode (15-dns-resolver ka approach) -- justified jab proxy ko apne clients ke liye format control chahiye ho ya jab record content inspect karna ho. Partial decode with compression-pointer REWRITING bhi possible hai, par woh extra complexity hai jiski yahan zaroorat nahi.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Query volume badhne se yeh decision affected nahi hota -- yeh per-packet correctness decision hai, throughput se independent. 10x/100x traffic par bottleneck cache hit rate aur upstream latency honge, rdata decoding approach nahi.
advanced.production_improvements: Agar kabhi CNAME-aware blocking/allowlisting chahiye ho (Stage 2 ka allowlist sirf query name match karta hai), ek SEPARATE, carefully-tested name-decoder likhna padega jo sirf is ONE purpose ke liye rdata ke andar ka compressed name decode kare -- bina poora packet rebuild kiye, bina us name ko kahin wapas likhe.

question: Why does BlockList use a trie over reversed dot-labels instead of a Set<string> of full domain names?
answer_hinglish:
Dono approach same rule de sakte hain -- 'exact domain ya uski koi subdomain block'. Farak hai COST mein. Ek Set mein har query ke liye tumhe har ANCESTOR check karna padta: isBlocked("x.y.ads.example.com") pehle poora string "x.y.ads.example.com" hash karega, miss hone par "y.ads.example.com", phir "ads.example.com", wagera -- har level ek NAYA string allocation aur ek NAYA hash, aur koi sharing nahi hoti entries ke beech.

Trie isko ek baar mein solve karta hai: query ke labels ko TLD se reverse order mein walk karo (com -> example -> ads), ek map lookup per label, aur jaise hi koi node 'blocked' mila, turant true return karo. Ek real tracker blocklist mein hazaaron subdomains ek hi common domain (jaise doubleclick.net) ke hote hain -- trie mein woh sab ek hi 'doubleclick -> net' path SHARE karte hain, Set mein har ek apna poora alag string carry karta.

Yeh choice specifically us INPUT SHAPE ke liye cheaper hai jo ek real ad/tracker list ki hoti hai: large size, deep subdomains, bahut sari shared suffixes. Chhote lists ke liye farak negligible hota, par yeh project ek real list ke liye design kiya gaya hai.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate data-structure choice ko INPUT SHAPE ke against justify kar sakta hai, sirf Big-O nahi bolta -- real blocklists ka shape (shared suffixes) is decision ka asli reason hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek library mein books ko exact title se ek flat list mein dhoondna vs ek classification tree (genre -> author -> series) se navigate karna -- tree mein shared branches ek hi baar store hote hain, flat list mein har book apna poora path carry karti hai.
how_it_works: add() labels ko REVERSE order (TLD first) mein trie mein walk/create karta hai aur last node ko blocked=true karta hai. isBlocked() same order mein walk karta hai aur jaise hi koi intermediate node blocked mile, true return kar deta hai -- matlab ek shorter blocked domain ka subtree ek longer query ko automatically cover kar leta hai.
in_this_project: src/blocklist.ts ka labelsOf domain ko lowercase karke split karta hai; add() labels.length-1 se 0 tak loop karta hai (TLD-first insertion); isBlocked() same reverse walk karta hai aur node.blocked true milte hi return true karta hai.
advantages: Shared suffixes memory mein ek hi baar store hote hain
Lookup query ke labels ki length mein linear hai, extra string allocation ke bina
'exact name OR any subdomain' rule free milta hai, special-case code ki zaroorat nahi
disadvantages: Set se thoda zyada code complexity (trie node management)
Chhoti blocklists (jaise 10-20 domains) ke liye farak practically zero hai
common_mistakes: Set approach ko 'simpler hai isliye better hai' maan lena bina input shape (large list, shared suffixes) consider kiye
Trie insertion LEAF-first (TLD last) kar dena -- isse subdomain-blocking rule automatically nahi milta
follow_up_questions: What is the memory footprint difference between a trie and a Set for a million-domain blocklist?
Why does inserting labels TLD-first matter for the subdomain-blocking rule?
Stage 2 allowlisting ke liye isi trie class ka doosra instance kyun reuse hua, har node par naya 'allowed' marker kyun nahi?

question: What is the difference between the 'nxdomain' and 'sinkhole' block modes, and why does this project support both instead of picking one?
answer_hinglish:
Dono modes ek blocked domain ke liye alag jawab dete hain. 'nxdomain' mode technically correct answer deta hai -- NXDOMAIN, matlab 'yeh naam exist hi nahi karta'. 'sinkhole' mode ek LIE deta hai -- ek normal-dikhne-wala A record (default 0.0.0.0) jaise woh domain exist karta ho aur resolve ho gaya ho.

Dono ke apne downside hain, aur yeh Pi-hole ka apna real, unresolved design debate hai isliye yeh project bhi configurable rakha hai, hardcode nahi kiya. NXDOMAIN 'correct' hai par kuch client software (browsers, apps) NXDOMAIN ko 'try again' jaisa treat karte hain aur AGGRESSIVELY retry karte hain -- ek blocked ad request retries ke burst mein badal sakta hai. Sinkhole IP ek lie hai, par zyada clients ek normal-dikhne-wala answer final maan lete hain aur retry nahi karte -- kam network noise.

Is project mein sinkholing SIRF A query types ke liye implement hai; har doosra type (AAAA, MX, TXT, ...) dono modes mein NXDOMAIN hi paata hai, kyunki AAAA ya doosre record types banane ka encoder yahan likha hi nahi gaya (scope cut, PLAN.md mein documented).
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate ek 'do options, dono valid' design decision ko samajh sakta hai bina 'ek hi sahi answer hona chahiye' mindset ke, aur client-behavior ka awareness bhi dikhata hai (retry storms).
real_world_analogy: Ek dukaan band hai batane ke do tareeke -- ek board 'yeh dukaan yahan kabhi thi hi nahi' (NXDOMAIN) vs ek board 'dukaan khuli hai' par andar kuch bhi nahi hai (sinkhole) -- pehla confusing lag sakta hai kuch logon ko (woh wapas aake dekhenge), dusra clearly 'kuch nahi milega' bata deta hai bina confusion ke.
how_it_works: buildBlockResponse mode aur query type check karta hai: mode === "nxdomain" ya type !== A hone par NXDOMAIN encode hota hai; sinkhole mode mein A query ke liye encodeARecord se ek real A record ban kar NOERROR ke saath jaata hai.
in_this_project: src/proxy.ts ka buildBlockResponse method yeh logic implement karta hai: `if (this.mode === "nxdomain" || q.type !== TYPE.A) return NXDOMAIN response`, warna sinkholeAddress (default "0.0.0.0") se encodeARecord ban kar NOERROR response banta hai, sinkholeTtl (default 60s) ke saath.
advantages: NXDOMAIN protocol-correct hai, honest signal deta hai
Sinkhole IP kam client-side retries trigger karta hai
disadvantages: NXDOMAIN kuch clients mein retry storms bana sakta hai
Sinkhole IP ek lie hai -- client ko lagta hai jaise resolve hua
common_mistakes: Yeh sochna ki sinkhole mode HAR query type ko sinkhole karta hai -- sirf A queries, baaki NXDOMAIN hi paate hain
sinkholeAddress ko hardcoded 0.0.0.0 maan lena -- yeh actually configurable hai
follow_up_questions: Why is sinkholing only implemented for A queries, not AAAA or others?
What client-side behavior difference have you seen between NXDOMAIN and a sinkhole response in practice?
What would a sinkholeAddress of 127.0.0.1 instead of 0.0.0.0 change for the client?

question: Why does ResponseCache use lazy expiry (checked only on read) instead of a background sweep timer that proactively removes expired entries?
answer_hinglish:
Yeh same reasoning hai jo is repo mein 23-password-manager ke session idle timeout mein use hoti hai: ek background sweep ko apna LIFECYCLE chahiye hota -- kaun ise start kare, kaun stop kare (process exit par), aur jab koi request nahi aa rahi tab bhi woh clock se time poochta rahega. Yeh real design aur testing cost hai ek benefit ke liye jiski yahan zaroorat nahi.

Lazy expiry mein, ek expired entry sirf 'miss' jaisa treat hota hai next time jab koi exact (name, type) ke liye dobara poochta hai -- get() check karta hai expiresAt <= now, aur agar expired hai toh usi lookup mein delete kar deta hai. Agar koi entry kabhi dobara nahi poocha jaata, woh thodi der extra memory mein baithi rehti hai -- koi harm nahi, kyunki woh kisi ko galat answer nahi de rahi.

Ek real risk hai: expired-aur-never-looked-up-again entries forever memory mein reh sakti hain. Isko maxEntries (default 10,000, oldest-insertion-first eviction) se bound kiya gaya hai -- same safety valve jo 15-dns-resolver ke cache mein hai. Toh lazy expiry + a bounded eviction policy dono combine karke ek simple, timer-free design deta hai jo correctness compromise nahi karta.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate lazy vs eager/background cleanup ka trade-off samajhta hai, aur yeh bhi ki lazy approach ka ONE real downside (unbounded memory) ko kaise bound kiya jaata hai (maxEntries).
real_world_analogy: Fridge mein expired items -- koi daily inspector nahi aata check karne; jab tum fridge kholte ho aur us item ko use karna chahte ho, tab hi dekhte ho expire ho gaya ya nahi. Agar koi item kabhi touch hi nahi hota, woh andar baitha rehta hai -- tabhi tak theek hai jab tak fridge full na ho jaaye.
how_it_works: get(k) pehle entries.get(k) karta hai; agar entry mili aur expiresAt <= clock.now(), toh entries.delete(k) karke undefined return karta hai -- yeh delete SIRF isi lookup ki wajah se hota hai. maxEntries ko evict() private method se enforce kiya jaata hai, har put() ke baad, jo oldest-insertion-order entry delete karta hai jab tak size <= maxEntries na ho jaaye.
in_this_project: src/cache.ts ka get() method lazy-eviction karta hai; put() delete-then-set pattern use karta hai (`this.entries.delete(k)` phir `this.entries.set(k, ...)`) taaki Map ki insertion-order iteration (jo evict() use karta hai) age order mein consistent rahe.
advantages: Koi timer lifecycle manage karne ki zaroorat nahi (start/stop/clock-source)
Code simple aur testable (ManualClock se deterministic)
Zero cost jab tak koi query actually us expired entry ko hit nahi karta
disadvantages: Ek never-requeried expired entry memory mein baithi reh sakti hai jab tak eviction na ho
Current cache size ka 'actually valid entries' count sirf lookup se pata chalta hai, proactively nahi
common_mistakes: Yeh sochna ki lazy expiry 'bug' hai kyunki expired data 'reh' jaata hai -- woh kabhi return nahi hota, sirf memory mein baitha hota hai
maxEntries ke bagair lazy expiry implement karna -- tab unbounded memory growth ka real risk ban jaata
follow_up_questions: What is the one real downside of lazy expiry, and how does this project bound it?
Why does put() delete the key before re-setting it, even on a fresh insert?
At what point would you reconsider adding a background sweep?

question: Why is this proxy's upstream-facing threat model deliberately narrower than 15-dns-resolver's, and what single check does it still keep?
answer_hinglish:
15-dns-resolver ek ITERATIVE resolver hai -- woh arbitrary authoritative servers se baat karta hai jinse usne pehle kabhi baat nahi ki, aur isliye har UDP query ko RANDOM source port AND random transaction ID se defend karna padta hai (Kaminsky-style spoofing defence) -- warna koi attacker guess karke fake answer inject kar sakta hai.

Yeh proxy sirf EK configured, TRUSTED upstream se baat karta hai (jaise 1.1.1.1, wahi role jo woh Pi-hole ke liye play karta hai). Yeh ek genuinely DIFFERENT threat model hai -- hum ek baar choose karte hain kis par trust karna hai (configuration time par), aur phir uske against poora Kaminsky-spoofing defence reproduce karne ki zaroorat nahi, kyunki attacker ko humare upstream ka exact traffic predict karna padega, jo already ek narrower problem hai.

Phir bhi EK cheap check kept hai, kyunki free hai: queryUdp mein, jab bhi koi UDP packet aata hai, uska rinfo.address aur rinfo.port configured upstream ke EXACT address/port se match hona chahiye, warna silently ignore karte hain (bina fail kiye, wait karte rehte hain). ID/QR match ek ALAG layer par, decoded reply par, proxy.ts mein hota hai -- mismatch hone par SERVFAIL, relay nahi.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate threat models ko CONTEXT-dependent samajhta hai -- 'random source port+ID' security best practice HAR situation mein zaroori nahi, agar threat model khud narrower hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek courier jo sirf ek TRUSTED warehouse se packages leta hai (sender ki identity ek baar verify karo, phir trust karo) vs ek courier jo kisi bhi anjaan sender se package le sakta hai (har baar full identity verification chahiye, kyunki koi bhi ho sakta hai).
how_it_works: queryUdp ke sock.on("message") handler mein pehla check hi yeh hai: `if (rinfo.address !== to.host || rinfo.port !== to.port) return;` -- matching nahi hua toh packet drop, listener wapas wait karta hai. Yeh check UDP socket level par hai; ID/QR verification isse ALAG, decoded reply par, proxy.ts ke handle() mein hoti hai.
in_this_project: src/transport.ts ka queryUdp ek address/port check karta hai har incoming UDP message par. src/proxy.ts ka handle() alag se `if (!parsed.header.qr || parsed.header.id !== rawHeader.id) throw new WireError(...)` karta hai -- yeh dono checks mil kar is narrower threat model ko implement karte hain.
advantages: Kaminsky-style full defence (random port+ID) ka implementation aur testing cost nahi uthana padta
Still ek cheap, free check kept hai jo wrong-sender packets ignore karta hai
disadvantages: Agar configured upstream khud compromise ho jaaye, yeh proxy use fully trust karta hai
Agar kabhi iterative resolution add karni ho (arbitrary servers se baat), yeh narrower model insufficient ho jaayega
common_mistakes: Yeh sochna ki source-address check hi poora spoofing defence hai -- yeh sirf ek NARROWER threat model ke liye kaafi hai, open-internet ke liye nahi
ID/QR check ko address check se duplicate/redundant samajhna -- yeh do ALAG layers hain, UDP socket level vs decoded application level
follow_up_questions: If this proxy ever started talking to arbitrary upstream servers (like adding iterative resolution), what would need to change?
Why is the ID/QR check done on the decoded reply in proxy.ts rather than inside queryUdp itself?
What does TRANSPORT1's mutation gap (wrong-source check never exercised) teach about testing a defence that never gets triggered in normal tests?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Single-trusted-upstream model ek cheap check (address/port match) ke saath kaafi hai; open-internet iterative resolution model ko random source port + random ID dono chahiye, jo extra socket management aur test complexity laata hai.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar configured upstream ka IP kisi tarah se spoof ho jaaye (jaise network-level MITM), yeh proxy us spoofed answer ko bina kisi aur check ke trust kar lega -- is design ka explicit accepted risk hai, kyunki upstream khud 'trusted' maana gaya hai.
advanced.alternatives: Random source port per query (already implicit, kyunki har query naya ephemeral socket leta hai) + random/unpredictable transaction ID handling jaisa 15-dns-resolver karta hai -- yeh add kiya ja sakta hai agar threat model badal jaaye.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Query volume se yeh threat model change nahi hota -- yeh ek per-upstream-relationship decision hai, traffic volume se independent.
advanced.production_improvements: Agar multiple upstreams add karne ho (failover ke liye), har upstream ke address/port check ko separately maintain karna hoga, aur yeh decide karna hoga ki kya sab upstreams equally 'trusted' hain ya kisi ko extra verification chahiye.

question: Why does forwardQuery open a brand-new ephemeral UDP socket for every query instead of sharing one long-lived socket across all forwarded queries?
answer_hinglish:
Ek long-lived shared socket (jaisa 15-dns-resolver use karta hai, jo MANY concurrent lookups ko ek hi socket se serve karta hai) ko IDs ko REWRITE karna padta hai -- kyunki ek hi socket par multiple in-flight queries ho sakti hain, aur incoming replies ko match karne ke liye unique IDs chahiye, jo client ke apne IDs se clash kar sakte hain.

Yahan, har forwarded query apna ALAG, FRESH UDP socket leta hai jo bind hota hai, exactly ek query bhejta hai, exactly ek reply (ya timeout) ka wait karta hai, phir close ho jaata hai. Isliye multiplexing ka koi concept hi nahi hai -- ek socket par kabhi do queries overlap nahi karti. Isse client ka ORIGINAL transaction ID bina rewrite kiye seedha forward kiya ja sakta hai, aur reply bhi usi ID ke saath relay ho jaata hai.

Trade-off yeh hai: har query ek naya socket bind/close karta hai (thoda overhead, OS-level socket creation), par exchange mein ID-rewriting logic, ek pending-queries map, aur concurrent-request bookkeeping -- yeh sab complexity nahi chahiye. Query volume jo yeh proxy expect karta hai (ek ghar/office ka DNS traffic) ke liye yeh overhead negligible hai.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate socket-per-request vs shared-pooled-socket trade-off samajhta hai, aur yeh bhi ki ID rewriting sirf MULTIPLEXING ki zaroorat hoti hai, inherent requirement nahi.
real_world_analogy: Ek disposable phone line jo sirf EK call ke liye use hoti hai vs ek shared call-center line jahan operator ko track karna padta hai kaunsi call kiske saath associated hai -- disposable line simple hai par thoda zyada setup cost per call.
how_it_works: queryUdp() har call par `dgram.createSocket("udp4")` karta hai, bind(0, ...) se ek free ephemeral port leta hai, query bhejta hai, reply ka wait karta hai (ya timeout), aur finish() mein sock.close() karta hai -- socket ka lifecycle exactly ek query-response cycle ke barabar hai.
in_this_project: src/transport.ts ke queryUdp mein har invocation apna naya dgram socket banata hai; koi socket pooling ya reuse nahi hai. forwardQuery() bhi client ki original id wali query buffer seedha forward karta hai, kabhi id rewrite nahi karta.
advantages: Client ka transaction id bina rewrite kiye forward hota hai -- simpler mapping logic
Koi pending-queries tracking map ki zaroorat nahi
Har query ka lifecycle independent aur isolated hai
disadvantages: Har query par socket create/bind/close overhead (small office traffic ke liye negligible)
High-throughput shared-infrastructure resolver ke liye yeh approach scale nahi karega
common_mistakes: Yeh sochna ki ID rewriting ALWAYS zaroori hoti hai DNS forwarding mein -- sirf jab socket SHARED/multiplexed ho
Ephemeral-socket-per-query ko 'inefficient' bol dena bina context ke -- yeh is project ke expected traffic volume ke liye sahi trade-off hai
follow_up_questions: What would need to change if this proxy needed to handle thousands of concurrent queries per second?
Why does a shared long-lived socket need to rewrite transaction IDs but an ephemeral-per-query socket does not?
What is the actual OS-level cost of creating and closing a UDP socket per query?

question: Why does ResponseCache store raw response bytes plus TTL byte offsets, instead of storing a parsed/structured representation of the cached answer?
answer_hinglish:
Yeh seedha us bade decision se juda hai jo poore project ka foundation hai: rdata ko kabhi decode nahi karna, kyunki uske andar DNS-compressed names ho sakti hain jo sirf ORIGINAL packet bytes ke relative valid hoti hain. Agar cache ek PARSED/structured representation store karta (jaise `{ name, type, ttl, rdata: parsedObject }`), toh ek cache hit ko serve karne ke liye us parsed object ko WAPAS encode karna padta -- aur wahi re-encoding risk wapas aa jaata jo relay decision ne avoid kiya tha.

Raw bytes store karna matlab cache hit ekdum CHEAP hai: ek Buffer copy, chaar TTL fields ko in-place patch karna (jo fixed-position integers hain, koi compression nearby nahi), aur 2-byte transaction id patch karna. Koi re-encoding step hi nahi hai, isliye koi naya corruption risk introduce nahi hota.

ttlOffsets store karne ki zaroorat isliye hai ki TTL countdown karne ke liye humein pata hona chahiye KAHAN woh 4-byte field hai buffer mein -- yeh wire.ts ke decodeResponse ne already decode time par record kiya tha (AnswerMeta.ttlOffset), toh cache.ts use sirf STORE karta hai aur get() time par use karta hai, dobara decode karne ki zaroorat nahi.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate consistently ek design principle (raw-bytes-only, never re-encode) ko DIFFERENT subsystems (transport AND cache) mein apply kar sakta hai, aur yeh samajhta hai ki 'structured storage' hamesha better nahi hota.
real_world_analogy: Ek photocopy machine jo original document ki EXACT copy rakhti hai (bas date-stamp update karti hai har copy par) vs ek machine jo document ko re-type karke naya banati hai -- re-typing mein typo/formatting errors introduce hone ka risk hai jo exact-copy mein nahi hota.
how_it_works: Entry interface mein buf (raw Buffer), expiresAt, insertedAt, aur ttlOffsets (number[]) store hote hain. get() ek Buffer.from(e.buf) copy banata hai, phir har offset par readUInt32BE/writeUInt32BE se TTL ko elapsed-seconds se countdown karta hai -- kabhi name ya rdata nahi touch karta.
in_this_project: src/cache.ts ka Entry interface `buf: Buffer` aur `ttlOffsets: number[]` rakhta hai (AnswerMeta.ttlOffset se derive hota hai proxy.ts mein). src/proxy.ts ka handle() `parsed.answers.map((a) => a.ttlOffset)` se yeh offsets cache.put() ko pass karta hai.
advantages: Koi re-encoding step nahi -- compression-pointer risk cache subsystem mein bhi nahi aata
Cache hit cheap hai: ek buffer copy + chaar integer patches
Cache aur transport dono EK SAME design principle follow karte hain (consistency)
disadvantages: Cache khud response ke content ko inspect/query nahi kar sakta (jaise 'kitne A records cached hain is IP ke against')
ttlOffsets ko decode time par hi record karna padta hai -- cache khud yeh compute nahi kar sakta
common_mistakes: Yeh sochna ki structured storage 'better design' hai by default -- yahan woh ek NAYA corruption risk introduce karta
ttlOffsets ko cache ke andar recompute karne ki koshish karna -- yeh decode time par hi sahi context (ttlOffset) available hota hai
follow_up_questions: What would break if the cache tried to re-encode a structured representation instead of patching raw bytes?
Why must ttlOffsets be computed at decode time, not inside the cache itself?
What is the one thing a raw-bytes cache fundamentally cannot do that a structured cache could?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Raw-bytes cache consistency ke saath trade hota hai introspection ke against -- cache content ko kabhi query/filter nahi kar sakte without re-decoding, par correctness guarantee strong hai.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar koi future change cache ko structured data store karne laga aur re-encoding add ki without a compression-pointer-safe encoder, toh wahi silent corruption bug wapas aa sakta hai jo relay decision ne avoid kiya tha -- par ab cache subsystem mein, jo debug karna aur harder hoga kyunki cache hit aur forward path alag code paths hain.
advanced.alternatives: Structured cache with a FULL, correct re-encoder (compression-pointer aware) -- possible but significant extra engineering effort for a benefit (content introspection) this project does not need.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Raw-bytes approach cache hit cost ko O(number of TTL offsets) rakhta hai, jo bahut chhota hai (typically 1-5 answers) -- yeh scale karta hai bina kisi change ke 10x/100x traffic tak.
advanced.production_improvements: Agar kabhi query-time analytics chahiye (jaise 'top cached domains'), ek SEPARATE lightweight metadata index (name, type, hit count) rakhna better hoga bajaye cache ke raw-bytes design ko badalne ke.

question: What would you add to this project before pointing it at a real home or office network's DNS traffic?
answer_hinglish:

Teesra: MONITORING -- proxy.stats already blocked/allowed/cacheHits/forwarded/servfail counters rakhta hai in-memory, par production mein yeh persist/export honi chahiye (jaise Prometheus metrics ya periodic log line) taaki koi dekh sake system healthy hai ya nahi. Chautha: upstream ko real resolver (1.1.1.1 jaisa) point karna, aur server ko network ka actual DNS bana ke clients ko point karna (router ya DHCP se).

question: After deploying this as the office's DNS, people say 'the internet feels slow.' What do you check first, in what order?
answer_hinglish:
Pehla check: proxy.stats se CACHE HIT RATE dekho (cacheHits / (cacheHits + forwarded)). Agar hit rate low hai, matlab zyada queries HAR BAAR upstream tak jaa rahi hain -- aur upstream round-trip hi latency ka sabse bada source hai (local cache lookup microseconds mein hota hai, UDP round-trip milliseconds mein). Low hit rate ka common reason: TTLs bahut chhote hain (upstream khud short TTL deta hai), ya traffic pattern mein bahut sare UNIQUE domains hain (kam repeat queries).

Doosra check: UPSTREAM LATENCY khud -- agar proxy ka configured upstream (jaise 1.1.1.1) khud slow respond kar raha hai ya udpTimeoutMs (default 2000ms) ke close chal raha hai, toh har forward query us latency ko client tak PASS karta hai. Yeh network-level issue ho sakta hai (ISP, routing) ya upstream resolver khud overloaded ho sakta hai.

Teesra: TCP-FALLBACK RATE -- agar bahut sari replies truncated (TC=1) aa rahi hain, toh har aisi query do round-trips leti hai (UDP attempt + TCP retry), jo TOTAL latency double kar deta hai us query ke liye. Yeh ek unusual upstream ya ek unusually large-answer domain ka signal ho sakta hai. Chautha: servfail rate -- agar high hai, clients khud apna fallback/retry logic trigger kar rahe honge, jo PERCEIVED slowness barhata hai bina proxy ki fault ke.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate ek SYSTEMATIC debugging order follow kar sakta hai (cheapest/highest-signal check pehle), production metrics ko diagnose karne ke liye use kar sakta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek restaurant mein 'service slow hai' complaint aane par pehle dekhna chahiye kitchen queue (cache hit rate -- kitne orders repeat hain vs naye), phir supplier delivery time (upstream latency), phir kitne orders complex/multi-step hain (TCP fallback), phir kitne orders cancel ho rahe hain (servfail).
how_it_works: proxy.stats.{blocked, cacheHits, forwarded, servfail} directly inspectable hain. TCP-fallback rate directly stats mein nahi hai (forwarded dono UDP aur TCP results ko count karta hai) -- yeh StubUpstream.calls[].transport jaisa concept production mein instrument karna padega, ya transport.ts mein ek counter add karna hoga.
in_this_project: src/proxy.ts ka ProxyStats interface sirf total/blocked/allowed/cacheHits/forwarded/servfail track karta hai -- TCP-fallback ka alag counter nahi hai abhi, yeh ek production improvement hoga. src/transport.ts ka forwardQuery hi woh jagah hai jahan UDP-vs-TCP decision hota hai.
advantages: Existing stats counters already deepest diagnosis ka base dete hain
Systematic check order time bachaata hai incident ke dauraan
disadvantages: TCP-fallback rate aur per-query upstream latency abhi instrumented nahi hain -- add karna padega
In-memory stats process restart par reset ho jaate hain, historical trend nahi milta
common_mistakes: Seedha upstream ko blame kar dena bina cache hit rate dekhe -- agar hit rate khud low hai, upstream perfectly fine ho sakta hai
udpTimeoutMs ko bina diagnosis badha dena -- isse genuine timeouts bhi lamba lagenge, symptom chhupa dega
follow_up_questions: How would you add a TCP-fallback-rate counter without changing forwardQuery's return type?
What would a low cache hit rate combined with low upstream latency tell you that a low hit rate with HIGH upstream latency would not?
What historical data would you want that in-memory stats cannot give you?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: In-memory-only stats simple hai par ek incident ke dauraan sirf 'abhi ka snapshot' deta hai -- time-series metrics (export to Prometheus/Grafana) chahiye hote agar trend dekhna ho ('kab se slow hua').
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar upstream resolver khud intermittently slow ho (jaise kuch seconds ke liye), udpTimeoutMs ke near-boundary queries SERVFAIL ho sakti hain inconsistently -- symptom 'kabhi slow kabhi normal' dikhega, jo diagnose karna harder hai without latency histograms.
advanced.alternatives: Ek dedicated metrics library (jaise prom-client) integrate karke per-query latency histogram, cache hit rate gauge, aur TCP-fallback counter expose karna -- yeh proper observability deta hai is quick in-memory-stats approach se zyada.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 10x traffic par, agar cache hit rate same rahe, upstream load bhi 10x badhega -- yeh upstream ka SPOF bana sakta hai. 100x par multiple upstreams/failover zaroori ho jaayega.
advanced.production_improvements: Per-query timing instrumentation add karo (start time capture karo handle() mein, end time forward/cache-hit path par), aur un latencies ko histogram ya percentile metrics mein expose karo -- sirf counters se latency distribution nahi dikhta.

question: How would you do capacity planning for running this DNS sinkhole on a small office network of, say, 150 employees?
answer_hinglish:
Capacity planning ke teen main resources hain: QUERY VOLUME, MEMORY (cache + blocklist), aur UPSTREAM connections. 150 employees ke liye, ek rough estimate: har device (laptop, phone) auto-refresh/background apps ki wajah se easily 50-200 DNS queries/hour generate karta hai peak time par -- 150 logon ke 2-3 devices each maan ke, roughly 300-450 devices, toh peak load kuch sau queries/second tak jaa sakta hai bursts mein (normal average bahut kam hoga).

MEMORY: cache ka maxEntries default 10,000 hai -- ek office ke unique (name, type) combinations easily is range mein fit ho jaate (common domains bahut REPEAT hote hain). Blocklist agar real curated list ho (jaise lakhs of domains), trie structure memory-efficient hai shared-suffix design ki wajah se, par ek rough number: lakh domains ka trie kuch dus MB range mein reasonable hona chahiye (exact number list ki shape par depend karta hai).

UPSTREAM: ek SINGLE ephemeral-socket-per-query design matlab upstream ko EK saath bahut saari concurrent UDP sockets khulti hain peak par -- OS ki ephemeral port range (typically 32768-60999 ya configured range) ek natural ceiling hai, par normal office load is limit ke paas nahi aayega. Agar query volume genuinely high ho (jaise 10,000+ qps), cache hit rate hi sabse bada lever hoga -- upstream ko kam se kam hit karna.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate rough-but-reasoned capacity estimates bana sakta hai (real numbers nahi maangta, par METHOD dekh raha hai), aur kis resource par bottleneck lagega yeh identify kar sakta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek office cafeteria ke liye kitchen capacity plan karna -- tumhe exact number nahi chahiye, par rough estimate (kitne log, kitni frequency, peak hours) se andaza lagana hota hai kitchen staff aur ingredients kitne chahiye.
how_it_works: maxEntries cache size cap hai (default 10,000, configurable via ResponseCacheOptions). Blocklist size trie node count se directly proportional hai domain entries ke, par SHARED suffixes ki wajah se raw domain count se kam nodes bante hain. Upstream ke liye koi explicit concurrency limit code mein nahi hai -- har forwarded query apna socket leta hai.
in_this_project: src/cache.ts ka ResponseCacheOptions.maxEntries (default 10_000) tune karne wala parameter hai. src/blocklist.ts ka BlockList trie structure hai jiska memory footprint domain count aur shared-suffix ratio par depend karta hai.
advantages: maxEntries already ek tunable safety cap hai
Trie design memory ko real blocklist shape ke liye already optimize karta hai
disadvantages: Koi built-in load-testing ya capacity benchmark is project mein nahi hai (97 tests correctness ke liye hain, load ke liye nahi)
Ephemeral-socket-per-query design high-qps scenarios mein OS limits hit kar sakta hai
common_mistakes: Exact numbers 'guarantee' karna bina load-testing kiye -- yeh estimates hain, measured capacity nahi
maxEntries ko bahut chhota rakhna 'memory bachane ke liye' -- isse cache hit rate drop hoga, jo latency ko worsen karega
follow_up_questions: How would you actually load-test this proxy before deploying it to 150 users?
What would you change if query volume turned out to be 10x your initial estimate?
Why might ephemeral-socket-per-query become a bottleneck at very high query volume?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Ephemeral-socket-per-query design simplicity ke liye optimized hai, high-throughput ke liye nahi -- socket-pooling/shared-socket design zyada qps handle kar sakta hai par ID-rewriting complexity ke saath.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar peak burst (jaise sab devices ek saath boot hote hain subah) query volume ko spike kare, aur ephemeral port range exhaust ho jaaye, naye forwardQuery calls fail ho sakte hain socket-bind errors ke saath -- yeh SERVFAIL ban jaayega clients ke liye, cascading slow-feeling symptom.
advanced.alternatives: Ek connection-pooled/shared UDP socket (ID-rewriting ke saath) high qps ke liye better scale karega. Multiple upstream resolvers ke beech load-balance karna bhi ek option hai agar single upstream bottleneck bane.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 150 se 1500 employees (10x) par, cache hit rate CRITICAL ho jaata hai -- maxEntries badhana padega, aur upstream load proportionally badhega jab tak hit rate improve na ho. 100x (15,000 employees) par yeh single-instance design shayad insufficient ho, horizontal scaling (multiple proxy instances, shared cache jaisa Redis) consider karna padega.
advanced.production_improvements: Ek load-testing script likho jo realistic query mix (repeat domains + unique domains ka ratio) simulate kare, aur proxy.stats se actual measured cache hit rate aur latency capture karo real traffic shape ke against, phir maxEntries aur upstream capacity ko measured data se tune karo, estimates se nahi.

question: What does allowNonLoopback actually guard against, and what would you still need before safely serving non-loopback clients?
answer_hinglish:
allowNonLoopback ek EXPLICIT opt-in flag hai SinkholeServer.listen() mein. Default behavior yeh hai ki server sirf loopback addresses (127.0.0.1, ::1, localhost, ya 127.x.x.x range) par bind ho sakta hai -- koi bhi doosra host try karne par server ek error throw karta hai, allowNonLoopback explicitly true kiye bina.

Reason README/server.ts dono mein likha hai: yeh proxy ki apna access control NAHI hai. Koi bhi client jo is server tak UDP packet bhej sakta hai, jawab paa sakta hai -- koi authentication, koi client-IP ACL, kuch nahi (yeh Stage 2 wale DOMAIN allowlist se bilkul alag cheez hai -- woh decide karta hai KAUNSA naam block na ho, yeh decide karta KAUN query kar sakta hai). Agar yeh non-loopback par bind ho jaaye bina kisi aur safeguard ke, yeh ek OPEN DNS RESOLVER ban jaata hai, jo DNS AMPLIFICATION attacks ka tool ban sakta hai (attacker spoofed source IP se chhota query bhejta hai, proxy bada response bhejta hai VICTIM ke address par).

Actually non-loopback clients (jaise ek office LAN ke doosre devices) ko safely serve karne ke liye sirf allowNonLoopback=true set karna kaafi NAHI hai -- tumhe ek firewall rule ya network-level ACL chahiye hoga jo sirf TRUSTED subnet se UDP:15353 traffic allow kare, warna proxy khud internet-facing amplification tool ban sakta hai agar galti se wrong interface par bind ho gaya.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate DNS amplification attacks samajhta hai, aur yeh bhi ki ek code-level guard (allowNonLoopback) network-level security (firewall/ACL) ka substitute nahi hai.
real_world_analogy: Ghar ka main door jo default LOCKED rehta hai (loopback-only) -- unlock karna (allowNonLoopback=true) sirf ek step hai; tumhe phir bhi decide karna hai KAUN aa sakta hai andar (firewall/ACL), warna unlocked door sabke liye khula hai.
how_it_works: isLoopback() function host string check karta hai (127.0.0.1, ::1, localhost, ya regex `/^127\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+$/`). listen() mein `if (!isLoopback(host) && !this.opts.allowNonLoopback) throw new Error(...)` -- yeh check bind() call se PEHLE hota hai.
in_this_project: src/server.ts ka isLoopback export function hai jo yeh check karta hai; listen() method us check ko enforce karta hai throw karte hue ek descriptive error message ke saath.
advantages: Default-safe: galti se open resolver bana dena mushkil hai
Error message explicitly reason bataata hai, operator ko guide karta hai
disadvantages: allowNonLoopback khud koi access control nahi deta -- sirf ek ADMISSION ki 'tum jaanbujh kar risk le rahe ho'
Network-level firewall/ACL alag se setup karna PADEGA, yeh flag khud kuch nahi karta
common_mistakes: Yeh sochna ki allowNonLoopback=true set karna 'safe non-loopback mode' enable karta hai -- yeh sirf guard HATATA hai, koi naya protection NAHI ADD karta
Firewall rules ke bina allowNonLoopback production mein use karna
follow_up_questions: What is a DNS amplification attack, and how would an open resolver enable one?
What firewall rule would you add before setting allowNonLoopback on an office network?
Why does the loopback check happen before bind() rather than being left to the OS?

question: What would you monitor in production using SinkholeProxy.stats, and what does each counter actually tell you?
answer_hinglish:
ProxyStats mein chhe counters hain: total, blocked, allowed (Stage 2), cacheHits, forwarded, servfail. Har ek ek ALAG health signal deta hai.

`total` baseline hai -- traffic volume kitna hai, overall. `blocked / total` ratio batata hai blocklist kitna EFFECTIVE hai (kitna traffic actually ad/tracker hai) -- agar yeh ratio suddenly drop kare, blocklist stale ho sakta hai ya naye trackers aa gaye hon jo list mein nahi hain. `cacheHits / (cacheHits + forwarded)` cache EFFICIENCY batata hai -- low hona matlab zyada upstream load aur zyada latency per query.

`allowed` batata hai kitni queries ne EXPLICITLY allowlist match kiya -- yeh exclusive bucket nahi hai, aisi query cacheHits ya forwarded mein bhi count hoti hai. Agar ek naya allowlist entry daala aur `allowed` nahi badha, entry galat hai ya woh naam koi query hi nahi kar raha. `forwarded` batata hai kitni queries actually upstream tak gayi -- yeh upstream LOAD ka direct proxy hai. `servfail / total` sabse IMPORTANT alert signal hai -- high servfail rate matlab upstream unreachable hai, ya timeout ho raha hai, ya koi malformed/mismatched reply aa rahi hai. Agar servfail spike ho, clients ko DNS resolution FAIL ho raha hai, jo unko ek 'internet down' jaisa feel karaata hai.

Production mein yeh 6 counters ko periodically (jaise har minute) SNAPSHOT lekar ek time-series store (Prometheus, CloudWatch, ya simple log lines) mein export karna chahiye, taaki trends dikhein -- ek single snapshot sirf 'abhi' bataata hai, trend 'kya badal raha hai' bataata hai.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate raw counters ko ACTIONABLE monitoring signals mein translate kar sakta hai, aur kaunsa counter kis FAILURE MODE ko surface karta hai yeh samajhta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek factory ke dashboard gauges -- total output (total), reject rate (blocked), rework rate (cacheHits vs forwarded), aur breakdown alarms (servfail) -- har gauge ek alag problem ko highlight karta hai.
how_it_works: Har counter handle() ke andar relevant branch mein increment hota hai: stats.total++ shuru mein, stats.allowed++ jab allowlist match ho (block check se pehle, additive), stats.blocked++ block path mein, stats.cacheHits++ cache-hit path mein, stats.forwarded++ successful-forward path mein, stats.servfail++ catch block mein.
in_this_project: src/proxy.ts ka handle() method har decision branch ke exact point par corresponding stats counter increment karta hai -- yeh single source of truth hai is proxy ke behavior ka real-time summary.
advantages: Counters already instrumented in the exact decision points, no guessing needed
Simple enough to export without touching core proxy logic
disadvantages: In-memory only -- process restart resets everything, no historical trend by default
No per-domain breakdown -- you know a block happened, not which domain was blocked most
common_mistakes: Sirf `total` ko dekhna aur dusre counters ignore karna -- total khud koi health signal nahi deta
servfail rate ko ignore karna jab tak user complaint na aaye -- yeh proactively alert hona chahiye
follow_up_questions: What threshold would you set for a servfail-rate alert, and why?
How would you add per-domain breakdown without significantly changing ProxyStats?
Why is total alone not a useful health signal?

question: The blocklist is loaded once at startup from a text file. What would periodic blocklist updates require, given the current design?
answer_hinglish:
Abhi BlockList ek trie hai jo constructor mein build hota hai aur SinkholeProxyOptions.blockList ke through proxy ko diya jaata hai -- yeh IMMUTABLE reference hai runtime par (no remove() method bhi exposed nahi hai, sirf add()). Config hot-reload explicitly PLAN.md mein 'Not in scope' list mein hai.

Simplest approach (code change ke bina): process ko PERIODICALLY restart karo ek updated blocklist file ke saath (jaise cron + systemd restart, ya PM2 jaisa process manager). Downside: restart ke dauraan thoda downtime hota hai (chhota, par real), aur in-flight queries drop ho sakti hain.

Actual hot-reload implement karne ke liye: ek NAYA BlockList instance banao naye file se, aur SinkholeProxy ke andar blockList reference ko ATOMICALLY SWAP karo (abhi yeh `readonly` hai proxy mein, toh yeh field ko mutable banana padega, ya proxy ko ek wrapper/indirection dena hoga jisse 'current blockList' lookup ho). Race condition se bachne ke liye swap ek single assignment honi chahiye (JS mein reference assignment already atomic hai single-threaded event loop mein), toh yeh actually straightforward hai -- bas `readonly` hatana aur ek reload() method add karna hoga jo file wapas parse kare.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate samajhta hai ki 'not implemented' feature ko add karne ke liye EXACT kaunsa existing constraint (readonly field) badalna padega, aur kya is single-threaded Node environment mein atomic swap simple hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek library ka entire catalog card-index replace karna -- agar tum ek NAYA index poora bana ke READY hone par ek hi jhatke mein purane ke JAGAH rakh do, users ko kabhi 'half-updated' catalog nahi dikhega.
how_it_works: Abhi `blockList` field SinkholeProxy mein `readonly` hai, constructor mein set hota hai. Hot-reload ke liye yeh field mutable banana hoga, aur ek public method (jaise reloadBlockList(path)) add karna hoga jo naya BlockList banaye aur this.blockList ko reassign kare.
in_this_project: src/proxy.ts ka SinkholeProxy class `readonly blockList: BlockList` field rakhta hai constructor-assigned. src/blocklist.ts ka loadBlockListFile already file-to-array parsing deta hai, sirf proxy-level wiring missing hai.
advantages: loadBlockListFile already does the hard part (parsing); only the swap mechanism is new
Reference swap is naturally atomic in a single-threaded event loop, no locking needed
disadvantages: Building a fresh large trie on every reload briefly doubles blocklist memory usage during the swap
No current mechanism to signal 'reload now' (would need a file watcher, a signal handler, or an admin endpoint)
common_mistakes: Mutating the existing BlockList in place (adding/removing entries one by one) instead of building a fresh one -- partial state could be visible mid-update in pathological cases
Forgetting that blockList is currently readonly -- a naive patch would not even compile
follow_up_questions: How would you trigger a reload: a file watcher, a cron-driven signal, or an admin API?
What happens to a query being handled at the exact moment the swap occurs?
Would you reload the cache too, or leave previously cached answers alone?

question: The configured upstream resolver goes down entirely. What happens right now, and what would you add for resilience?
answer_hinglish:
Abhi exactly EK upstream hai (SinkholeProxyOptions.upstream), aur agar woh poori tarah down ho jaaye, har forwardQuery call udpTimeoutMs (default 2000ms) tak wait karega, phir TimeoutError throw karega. proxy.ts ka handle() is error ko catch karta hai aur client ko SERVFAIL return karta hai -- koi hang nahi, koi crash nahi, bas har non-blocked, non-cached query SERVFAIL ban jaati hai jab tak upstream wapas na aaye.

Issue yeh hai ki EK bhi failure SINGLE POINT OF FAILURE ban jaata hai -- blocked queries aur cache hits (jo already cached hain) kaam karte rahenge (woh upstream ko touch hi nahi karte), par koi NAYI non-cached query fail hogi. Agar office ka traffic mostly fresh/unique domains ka hai, impact bada hoga; agar mostly repeat/cached domains hain, impact kam dikhega jab tak TTLs expire na ho jaayen.

Resilience ke liye: (1) MULTIPLE upstreams configure karna with a failover order -- agar primary timeout/error de, SECOND upstream try karo SAME query ke liye, forwardQuery ko ek list of Endpoints accept karne jaisa banana. (2) Health-check upstream periodically (background ping ya actual test query) taaki proxy KNOW kare upstream down hai PEHLE se, retry-per-query ke bajaye. (3) Stale-cache-serving: agar cache mein EXPIRED entry hai aur upstream down hai, ek expired-but-recent answer serve karna 'kuch nahi' se behtar ho sakta hai (though yeh ek deliberate trade-off hai, abhi project mein implement nahi hai).
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate single-upstream SPOF ko identify kar sakta hai, aur PRACTICAL failover strategies propose kar sakta hai jo existing architecture ke saath fit hon.
real_world_analogy: Ek dukaan jiska sirf EK supplier hai -- supplier ki factory band ho jaaye toh dukaan ka stock khatam ho jaata hai naye orders ke liye, par jo saaman already shelf par hai (cache) woh bikta rehta hai jab tak khatam na ho.
how_it_works: forwardQuery ek single Endpoint accept karta hai; queryUdp us EK address ko query bhejta hai aur timeout par TimeoutError throw karta hai. proxy.ts ka handle() ka catch block YEH error ko (aur koi bhi doosra throw) SERVFAIL mein convert karta hai, bina cache karte hue.
in_this_project: src/proxy.ts ka handle() method ka try/catch block forwardQuery ki har failure (TimeoutError, TransportError, WireError on mismatched reply) ko ek hi SERVFAIL path mein collapse karta hai. src/transport.ts ka Endpoint interface abhi singular hai, list nahi.
advantages: Current design fails SAFELY (SERVFAIL, never hang/crash) even with zero resilience added
Cache already shields previously-resolved domains from a short upstream outage
disadvantages: Single upstream is a hard SPOF for any non-cached query
No proactive health-check -- every query pays the full timeout cost during an outage
common_mistakes: Adding a second upstream but trying BOTH in parallel always -- wastes resources on the common case where the primary is healthy; sequential fallback is usually better
Forgetting that a failover still needs the SAME id/QR verification per upstream reply
follow_up_questions: Would you try upstreams sequentially or in parallel, and why?
How would a periodic health-check change the per-query timeout behavior during an outage?
Should an expired cache entry ever be served as a last resort when all upstreams are down?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Single-upstream design simplicity ke liye hai (Pi-hole jaisa ek resolver model) -- multi-upstream failover resilience deta hai par complexity badhata hai (kis upstream ko try karein pehle, health state track karna).
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar upstream down ho aur failover na ho, saari non-cached queries timeoutMs ke baad SERVFAIL hoti hain -- yeh user ko 'internet down' jaisa feel karaata hai, jab asal mein sirf DNS resolution fail ho raha hai, internet connectivity nahi.
advanced.alternatives: Sequential failover (primary -> secondary -> ...) sabse simple aur common hai. Health-checked failover (periodic background ping) proactive hai par extra complexity. Parallel race-all-upstreams fastest response deta hai par zyada resource use karta hai per query.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Traffic volume se yeh resilience concern independent hai -- yeh ek AVAILABILITY decision hai, throughput decision nahi. Zyada traffic matlab outage ka IMPACT bada (zyada failed queries), par mechanism same rahega.
advanced.production_improvements: Ek health-check background task add karo jo periodically upstream ko ek chhota test query bheje aur result track kare; forwardQuery ko ek Endpoint[] accept karne do with sequential fallback; aur SERVFAIL rate ko alert-triggering metric banao taaki outage automatically detect ho, user complaint se pehle.

question: Walk through SinkholeProxy.handle()'s exact control flow from a raw query buffer to a raw response buffer.
answer_hinglish:
handle() ek async function hai jo Buffer leta hai aur Buffer | undefined return karta hai. Step by step: (1) stats.total++ sabse pehle. (2) decodeHeader(buf) try karta hai -- fail hua (12 bytes se kam) toh undefined return (kuch answer nahi, kyunki header bhi nahi padh paaye). (3) agar rawHeader.qr true hai (yeh ek reply hai, query nahi), undefined return -- do servers ping-pong na karein.

(4) decodeQuery(buf) try karta hai -- WireError throw hua toh FORMERR response. (5) opcode check -- non-QUERY toh NOTIMP. (6) questions.length !== 1 ya missing toh FORMERR. (7) class !== IN toh NOTIMP. (8) canonicalName se name normalize karta hai.

(9) Stage 2: `allowed = this.allowList?.isBlocked(name) ?? false` -- match hua toh stats.allowed++. Phir `!allowed && blockList.isBlocked(name)` true hone par stats.blocked++ aur buildBlockResponse() return. (10) warna cache.get(name, q.type) check -- hit hone par stats.cacheHits++ aur patchId(cached, rawHeader.id) return (naye client ka id patch karke). (11) warna forwardQuery() call -- upstream se reply aata hai, decodeResponse se parse hota hai, id/qr verify hota hai, successful NOERROR+answers hone par cache.put() hota hai, stats.forwarded++, aur replyBuf raw return hota hai. (12) kisi bhi step mein forward/decode fail ho, catch block SERVFAIL return karta hai, stats.servfail++.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate ek non-trivial async decision function ko branch-by-branch trace kar sakta hai, exactly jaise code review mein karna padta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek airport security checkpoint ka flow -- ID check (header valid?), boarding pass check (valid query?), watchlist check (blocked?), already-cleared-today check (cache hit?), aur agar kuch nahi mila toh manual verification (forward to upstream).
how_it_works: Har branch ek specific RCODE ya path ko represent karta hai -- yeh ek early-return style function hai jo har invalid/special case ko jaldi handle karta hai before pahunchne forward logic tak.
in_this_project: src/proxy.ts ka handle() method exactly yeh sequence follow karta hai -- header decode, qr check, query decode, opcode/question/class validation, allowlist check, blocklist check, cache check, forward+cache-put, sab try/catch ke andar wrapped jisse koi bhi unexpected throw SERVFAIL mein convert ho jaaye.
advantages: Har branch ek specific, real-DNS-correct response deta hai -- koi silent swallow nahi
Pure buffer-in/buffer-out hai, isliye real sockets ke bina unit-testable
disadvantages: Function thoda lamba hai (ek function mein kaafi responsibilities) -- readability ke liye split kiya ja sakta tha, par cohesion high hai
common_mistakes: Yeh sochna ki blocklist check cache check ke BAAD hota hai -- actually blocklist PEHLE check hota hai, taaki blocked domain kabhi cache ya upstream ko touch na kare
cache.get() ka result directly return kar dena bina patchId() se naye client ka id patch kiye

question: How does decodeResponse read an answer record's TTL and its byte offset without touching its rdata?
answer_hinglish:
decodeResponse header aur questions decode karne ke baad, ancount jitni baar ek loop chalaata hai. Har iteration mein: pehle r.name() se record ka OWNER name padhta hai (jo compressed ho sakta hai, readName handle karta hai), phir r.u16() se type aur class padhta hai.

Yahan EK important line hai: `const ttlOffset = r.pos;` -- yeh TTL field SHURU hone se PEHLE current reader position capture kar leta hai. Phir `const ttl = r.u32("RR ttl")` call hoti hai, jo 4 bytes padhti hai AUR reader ko 4 positions aage badha deti hai. Isliye ttlOffset exactly woh byte position hai jahan se TTL ka 4-byte big-endian integer shuru hota hai buffer mein.

Uske baad `const rdlength = r.u16(...)` rdata ki length padhta hai, aur `r.skip(rdlength, "rdata")` us pure rdata ko bina ek byte bhi interpret kiye AAGE badha deta hai. Result: AnswerMeta object mein `ttl` (number value, computation ke liye) AND `ttlOffset` (byte position, cache.ts ko patching ke liye) dono available hote hain, bina rdata ko kabhi decode kiye.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate ek wire-format parser ke EXACT byte-level mechanics trace kar sakta hai, specifically yeh samajhta hai ki 'offset capture BEFORE read' pattern kyun kaam karta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek form mein ek specific blank field ka POSITION note karna (jaise 'yeh field page 2, line 5 par hai') bina us field ke VALUE ko interpret kiye -- baad mein sirf us exact position par jaake value overwrite kar sakte ho.
how_it_works: Reader class ka `pos` field current read position track karta hai. u32() internally pos ko 4 se increment karta hai read ke BAAD. Isliye `r.pos` ko u32() call se PEHLE capture karna EXACTLY TTL field ka start offset deta hai.
in_this_project: src/wire.ts ke decodeResponse loop mein `const ttlOffset = r.pos; const ttl = r.u32("RR ttl");` yeh sequence hai. Yeh ttlOffset AnswerMeta mein store hota hai aur proxy.ts se cache.ts tak pass hota hai TTL-countdown ke liye.
advantages: Offset capture simple aur cheap hai -- koi extra buffer scan nahi chahiye
TTL value AND offset dono mil jaate hain ek hi pass mein
disadvantages: Agar u16/u32 methods ka order kabhi badal jaaye (jaise koi field insert ho jaaye type aur ttl ke beech), offset calculation silently WRONG ho jaayega bina kisi obvious error ke
common_mistakes: r.pos ko u32() call ke BAAD capture karna -- isse ttlOffset accidentally rdlength field ki shuruaat point karega
Yeh sochna ki ttlOffset koi SEPARATE scan se compute hota hai -- yeh sirf reader ki current position hai, koi extra work nahi
follow_up_questions: What would happen if the code captured r.pos right after reading the TTL instead of right before?
Why is reading the name first (with its own variable-length compression) not a problem for computing a later fixed-offset field?
How does cache.ts use this offset when it later hands back a cached response?

question: Walk through how BlockList.add and BlockList.isBlocked actually walk the trie, label by label.
answer_hinglish:
labelsOf(domain) pehle domain ko trim+lowercase karta hai, trailing dot strip karta hai, aur phir '.' se split karke labels ka array deta hai (jaise 'ads.example.com' -> ['ads', 'example', 'com']). Empty labels (jaise do dots ek saath) RangeError throw karte hain.

add(domain): labels array ko REVERSE order mein walk karta hai, matlab `labels.length - 1` (jo 'com' hai) se shuru karke 0 (jo 'ads' hai) tak. Har label ke liye, current node ke children Map mein check karta hai -- nahi mila toh NAYA node banata hai aur map mein set karta hai, phir 'node' variable ko us child par move karta hai. Loop ke END mein, last reached node (jo 'ads' node hai) par `blocked = true` set hota hai.

isBlocked(name): SAME reverse-order walk karta hai, par har step par check karta hai `if (node.blocked) return true` -- yeh match karta hai agar WALK ke beech mein kabhi koi marked node mil jaaye, matlab query ek blocked domain ki subdomain hai. Agar koi child missing mila (map mein nahi hai), seedha `return false` -- query us blocked subtree mein hi nahi hai.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate ek trie ke insertion aur lookup logic ko LABEL-BY-LABEL trace kar sakta hai, specifically yeh samajhta hai ki REVERSE order insertion kyun subdomain-blocking rule ko 'free' deta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek directory path walk karna root se leaf tak (/com/example/ads) -- agar koi intermediate folder 'locked' maarka hai, uske andar ki har subfolder automatically 'locked' hai, chahe woh subfolder khud kabhi explicitly mark na ki gayi ho.
how_it_works: TrieNode interface `{ children: Map<string, TrieNode>; blocked: boolean }` hai. Reverse-order insertion matlab TLD (com) root ke sabse CLOSE hai, aur most-specific label (ads) sabse DEEP hai -- yahi property isBlocked() ko 'early return true' allow karti hai kyunki parent marking automatically child ko cover karti hai.
in_this_project: src/blocklist.ts ka labelsOf, add, aur isBlocked teen functions hain jo yeh implement karte hain -- add() ek for loop `for (let i = labels.length - 1; i >= 0; i--)` use karta hai, isBlocked() exact same loop structure use karta hai.
advantages: O(number of labels) insertion aur lookup, no extra allocation per ancestor
Subdomain-blocking rule automatic hai, reverse insertion order ki wajah se
disadvantages: Trie nodes ka Map-per-node overhead chhoti lists ke liye thoda zyada hai array/object ke comparison mein
common_mistakes: Labels ko FORWARD order (ads pehle, com last) insert kar dena -- isse subdomain-blocking rule TOOT jaata
isBlocked() mein `node.blocked` check ko loop ke BAAD karna instead of HAR step par -- isse sirf EXACT match hi detect hota, subdomains nahi
follow_up_questions: What would break if labels were inserted in forward order instead of reversed?
Why does isBlocked() check node.blocked inside the loop rather than only after it finishes?
How would you add an exact-match-only block mode alongside the current subdomain-inclusive mode?

question: Walk through exactly how forwardQuery's TC-bit check triggers the TCP retry path, down to the socket calls.
answer_hinglish:
forwardQuery sabse pehle `await queryUdp(to, query, opts.udpTimeoutMs, opts.onUdpBound)` call karta hai -- yeh ek Promise return karta hai jo UDP socket bind karta hai (ek ephemeral port par), query bhejta hai, aur ek matching reply (sahi address/port se) ka wait karta hai ya timeout hone par reject karta hai.

UDP reply mil jaane par, forwardQuery `decodeHeader(udpReply)` call karta hai -- yeh sirf 12-byte header peek karta hai (cheap operation), poora message decode nahi karta. Agar yeh header decode bhi fail ho jaaye (corrupt reply), WireError throw hota hai jo upar SERVFAIL mein convert hota hai proxy.ts mein.

Agar header successfully decode hua, `if (!header.tc) return udpReply;` check karta hai -- TC bit false hai toh UDP reply SEEDHA return hoti hai, kuch aur nahi hota. Par agar `header.tc` true hai (truncated), forwardQuery `return queryTcp(to, query, opts.tcpTimeoutMs)` call karta hai -- SAME exact query buffer ko, ek NAYE TCP connection par bhejta hai. queryTcp net.connect() karta hai, connect event par frameTcp(query) se 2-byte length-prefix laga ke query bhejta hai, aur LengthPrefixedReader se incoming TCP stream ko frames mein split karta hai jab tak poora reply na mil jaaye.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate DNS ke TC-bit-to-TCP-retry pattern ko sirf CONCEPT level par nahi, balki EXACT function-call sequence level par trace kar sakta hai -- yeh ek real network-protocol-implementation skill hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek chhoti parchi (UDP) par poora message nahi fit hua, toh sender bolta hai 'yeh incomplete hai, poora message ek bade packet (TCP) mein bhejta hoon' -- receiver same request ko ek ALAG, bade-capacity channel par dobara bhejta hai.
how_it_works: queryUdp aur queryTcp dono Promise-based hain with their own timeout/cleanup logic. forwardQuery dono ko SEQUENTIALLY await karta hai -- TCP retry sirf tab shuru hoti hai jab UDP reply SUCCESSFULLY mil gayi ho AUR uska TC bit set ho, timeout ke case mein TCP try nahi hoti (poori query hi TimeoutError throw kar degi).
in_this_project: src/transport.ts ka forwardQuery function yeh exact sequence implement karta hai: queryUdp -> decodeHeader (peek) -> TC check -> conditional queryTcp. queryTcp andar LengthPrefixedReader class use karta hai jo RFC 1035 4.2.2 ke 2-byte length-prefix framing ko handle karta hai.
advantages: TCP retry sirf jab genuinely zaroori ho (TC bit) tab hi trigger hoti hai -- no wasted TCP connections on normal replies
Same exact query buffer dono transports par bhejta hai, consistency guaranteed
disadvantages: TCP retry ek EXTRA round-trip latency add karti hai (connect + send + receive) upar UDP attempt ke
common_mistakes: Yeh sochna ki TCP retry PARALLEL mein UDP ke saath try hoti hai -- yeh actually SEQUENTIAL hai, UDP reply ke TC bit dekhne ke BAAD
decodeHeader ko poora decodeResponse samajh lena -- yeh sirf 12-byte header peek hai, cheap aur fast
follow_up_questions: Why does forwardQuery only peek the header (decodeHeader) rather than fully decoding the UDP reply before checking TC?
What happens if the UDP reply is valid but the subsequent TCP retry also fails?
Why is the same raw query buffer reused for the TCP retry instead of re-encoding it?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Sequential UDP-then-TCP-on-TC hai simplicity aur correctness ke liye optimal -- parallel racing UDP+TCP har query par resource-wasteful hota bina kisi real benefit ke, kyunki TC sirf UDP ke size-limit ki wajah se set hota hai.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar TCP retry bhi fail ho jaaye (upstream TCP port band hai, ya connection refused), forwardQuery us error ko propagate karega aur proxy.ts SERVFAIL return karega -- client ko pata nahi chalega ki UDP succeeded tha par TCP fail hua, sirf ek generic SERVFAIL milega.
advanced.alternatives: Kuch resolvers ALWAYS TCP try karte hain agar UDP EDNS buffer size exceed ho sakta ho (proactive), is project mein reactive approach hai (UDP try karo, TC dekhne par hi TCP karo) -- reactive simpler hai aur common-case (non-truncated) ke liye ek extra round-trip avoid karta hai.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Agar TCP-fallback rate high ho (jaise bahut sare large-answer domains), total latency per query double ho jaata hai un cases mein -- 10x traffic par yeh TCP connections ka volume bhi 10x karega, jo upstream par extra load daalta hai.
advanced.production_improvements: TCP-fallback rate ko ek alag stats counter mein track karo (abhi ProxyStats mein nahi hai) taaki production mein yeh pata chale kitna traffic double-round-trip pay kar raha hai, aur agar rate high ho toh upstream resolver provider se baat karo ki woh itne bade answers kyun de raha hai.

question: How does the Reader class in wire.ts make every read bounds-checked, and what happens when a read would run past the buffer?
answer_hinglish:
Reader class ek simple wrapper hai ek Buffer ke upar, jisme ek `pos` field current position track karta hai. Har read method (u8, u16, u32, skip) PEHLE `need(n, what)` call karta hai, jo check karta hai `this.pos + n > this.buf.length` -- agar yeh true hai, matlab buffer mein itne bytes hi nahi bache, toh WireError throw hota hai EXACT reason ke saath (kya field padhne ki koshish ho rahi thi, kitne bytes chahiye the, kahan se).

Isi wajah se koi bhi read method CRASH nahi karta array-index-out-of-bounds se -- JavaScript mein `buf[pos]` bounds se bahar hone par `undefined` deta hai silently, jo agar check na kiya jaaye toh galat data ban jaata (undefined ko number treat karna). need() yeh risk explicitly eliminate karta hai EK EXPLICIT throw ke through.

Har decode function (decodeQuery, decodeResponse, readName) ek Reader instance use karta hai, aur jahan bhi koi field truncated/missing mile, WireError propagate ho jaata hai upar tak, jahan caller (decodeQuery, decodeResponse, ya proxy.ts) use catch karke appropriate response deta hai (FORMERR, SERVFAIL, ya silent drop) -- kabhi process crash nahi hota ek malformed packet ki wajah se.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate samajhta hai ki untrusted network input ko parse karte waqt EXPLICIT bounds-checking zaroori hai, aur yeh ek reusable pattern (Reader class) ke through consistently enforce kiya ja sakta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek measuring tape jo khud bol de 'itni lambi nahi hai' agar tum usse zyada lamba kuch measure karne ki koshish karo, bajaye silently galat number dene ke.
how_it_works: need(n, what) ek guard hai jo HAR read se pehle call hota hai. u8/u16/u32 internally need() call karte hain phir Buffer ke readUInt16BE/readUInt32BE jaise built-in methods use karte hain, aur pos ko accordingly increment karte hain.
in_this_project: src/wire.ts ki Reader class ek private helper hai (class ke andar hi defined, exported nahi) jo decodeQuery, decodeResponse, aur readName sab use karte hain. Isi design ki wajah se 1500 random + 500 bit-flipped packets ka fuzz test (5 seeds) kabhi crash nahi karta, sirf WireError throw karta hai.
advantages: Har read consistently bounds-checked hai -- ek hi jagah (need()) mein logic hai, duplicated nahi
Error messages descriptive hain (what, kitne bytes, kahan) -- debugging easy ho jaati hai
disadvantages: Har read call par ek extra function call (need()) ka small overhead hai -- negligible par zero nahi
common_mistakes: Buffer ko directly index karna (buf[pos]) bina Reader use kiye -- yeh silently undefined de sakta hai bounds ke bahar
need() check ko read ke BAAD lagana instead of PEHLE -- tab tak galat data already use ho chuka hoga
follow_up_questions: What would happen if need() were called after reading instead of before?
Why does WireError include the offset and what was being read, rather than a generic message?
How does the fuzz test (1500 random + 500 bit-flipped packets) rely on this bounds-checking never crashing?

question: What does patchId do, and why is patching only the 2-byte transaction ID enough to safely reuse a cached response for a different client?
answer_hinglish:
patchId ek chhota helper function hai: `patchId(buf, id)` ek Buffer ki COPY banata hai (`Buffer.from(buf)`), uske first 2 bytes (jo DNS header ka id field hote hain) ko naye id se overwrite karta hai (`writeUInt16BE(id, 0)`), aur yeh naya buffer return karta hai -- ORIGINAL buffer kabhi mutate nahi hota.

Yeh enough hai kyunki DNS message ka transaction id SIRF ek matching mechanism hai -- client apna chuna hua id query mein bhejta hai, aur reply mein SAME id expect karta hai taaki woh confirm kar sake yeh reply USI ki query ka jawab hai. Iske aage DNS message mein kuch bhi id-DEPENDENT nahi hota -- questions, answers, sab apne aap mein complete hote hain, id sirf ek CORRELATION token hai.

Isliye jab cache.get() ek pehle-se-stored response return karta hai (jo kisi PURANE client ki id ke saath stored tha), handle() sirf patchId() se NAYE client ka id us copy mein likh deta hai -- baaki poora message (questions, answers, TTLs already countdown-patched) bilkul same reh sakta hai, kyunki woh id-independent hai.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate samajhta hai DNS transaction id ka EXACT purpose (correlation, not content), aur kyun ek cached response ko reuse karne ke liye sirf EK field patch karna kaafi hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek courier receipt jisme sirf tracking number badalta hai jab SAME package doosre customer ko bhi deliver karna ho (jaise ek bulk order ka hi copy) -- package ka content same rehta hai, sirf tracking number unique hota hai har recipient ke liye.
how_it_works: Buffer.from(buf) ek NAYI memory allocation karta hai aur bytes copy karta hai -- yeh zaroori hai taaki caller ka original buffer (jo ho sakta hai kisi aur context mein reference hai) kabhi accidentally mutate na ho. writeUInt16BE(id, 0) header ka pehla 2-byte field (id) overwrite karta hai, jo DNS wire format mein always offset 0 par hota hai.
in_this_project: src/proxy.ts ka patchId function handle() ke andar cache-hit path mein use hota hai: `return patchId(cached, rawHeader.id);` -- yeh current query ke rawHeader.id ko cached buffer mein patch karta hai.
advantages: Ek hi field patch karna hai -- cheap aur simple
Buffer.from() ki wajah se original cached buffer kabhi corrupt nahi hota
disadvantages: Agar yeh copy step miss ho jaaye, ek client ka patch dusre concurrent client ke liye bhi apply ho sakta tha (shared mutable state bug)
common_mistakes: Buffer.from() skip karke directly cached buffer ko mutate karna -- yeh agle hi cache.get() call ko galat id de dega
Yeh sochna ki id patch karne se answer/questions bhi 'match' karne chahiye kisi tarah -- yeh independent fields hain
follow_up_questions: What would go wrong if patchId mutated the buffer in place instead of copying it?
Why is the transaction id always at byte offset 0 in a DNS message?
Does the TTL-countdown patching in cache.ts also need to copy the buffer, and why?

question: Walk through readName's compression-pointer handling: how does it decode a pointer, and what stops it from looping forever on a malicious packet?
answer_hinglish:
readName ek buffer aur start offset leta hai, aur labels ko collect karta hai jab tak ek terminating zero byte ya ek compression pointer na mile. Har byte ka top 2 bits check hota hai (`len & 0xc0`): agar `0xc0` hai, yeh ek COMPRESSION POINTER hai -- next byte ke saath milke ek 14-bit target offset banta hai (`((len & 0x3f) << 8) | buf[pos + 1]`), jo batata hai 'baaki naam yahan se continue hota hai'.

Loop-protection ke DO independent rules hain. Pehla: `if (target >= runStart) throw` -- target hamesha us labels-run se STRICTLY PEHLE point karna chahiye jo ABHI padhi ja rahi hai (runStart). Yeh guarantee karta hai ki target HAMESHA ghat raha hai har jump par, isliye infinite loop MATHEMATICALLY impossible hai -- ek decreasing sequence of non-negative integers finite hoti hai.

Doosra: `if (++jumps > MAX_POINTER_JUMPS) throw` -- ek HARD CAP (32) bhi hai total jumps par, taaki even ek VALID-but-adversarial chain of decreasing pointers (jaise ek packet jisme 1000 chhote jumps ho) bahut lamba na chale. Dono rules MIL kar guarantee dete hain ki readName HAMESHA terminate karega, chahe packet jaisa bhi adversarial ho.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate DNS compression pointer handling ko EXACT bit-manipulation level par samajhta hai, aur yeh bhi ki SECURITY-CRITICAL loop-protection do INDEPENDENT guarantees se kyun banta hai (defense in depth).
real_world_analogy: Ek choose-your-own-adventure book jahan 'page 45 par jao' jaise instructions hain -- agar rule ho ki tum sirf PEHLE padhe hue page se PEHLE wale page par jaa sakte ho, tum kabhi loop mein nahi phasoge, kyunki page number hamesha ghatta rahega.
how_it_works: `runStart` variable current labels-run ka starting offset hold karta hai. Jab pointer follow hoti hai, `runStart = target` reset hota hai NAYE position par -- taaki AGLI pointer (agar ho) us NAYE position se compare ho, chain mein har jump progressively strict hota hai.
in_this_project: src/wire.ts ka readName function `target >= runStart` check (backward-only rule) aur `jumps > MAX_POINTER_JUMPS` (32-jump cap) dono implement karta hai. README ki wire.ts table explicitly '1-jump, 32-jump, 33-jump (rejected), self/forward pointer (rejected)' tests reference karti hai.
advantages: Backward-only rule MATHEMATICALLY guarantees termination, independent of any hardcoded limit
MAX_POINTER_JUMPS cap bounds worst-case work even within valid decreasing chains
disadvantages: Dono checks ek saath maintain karna thoda extra cognitive load hai samajhne ke liye (do independent invariants)
common_mistakes: Sirf MAX_POINTER_JUMPS cap par rely karna aur backward-only check skip kar dena -- yeh WIRE1 mutation jaisa gap chhod deta, jahan ek forward/self pointer ek SPECIFIC jump count ke bina bhi infinite-ish loop create kar sakta hai
`end` variable ko update karna HAR jump par instead of sirf FIRST jump par -- `end` client ko batana chahiye naam EXACT kahan khatam hua MESSAGE mein (pehli pointer ke baad), na ki jump ke baad kahan
follow_up_questions: Why are two independent loop-protection mechanisms (backward-only AND a jump cap) both kept, instead of just one?
What would a self-referencing or forward-pointing compression pointer do if the backward-only check were removed?
Why does `end` only get set on the FIRST pointer jump, not on subsequent ones?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Do independent checks (backward-only + jump cap) defense-in-depth hai -- agar ek rule mein koi subtle bug ho, doosra rule phir bhi protect karta hai. Sirf ek rule rakhna code chhota karta par single-point-of-failure security property bana deta.
advanced.failure_scenarios: WIRE1 mutation check exactly yeh prove karta hai: backward-only rule disable karne par, suite CAUGHT karta hai -- matlab koi test is rule ko specifically exercise karta hai, aur yeh rule REAL protection deta hai, decorative nahi.
advanced.alternatives: Kuch parsers sirf ek VISITED-OFFSETS set maintain karte hain (cycle detection) bajaye backward-only rule ke -- yeh bhi correct hai par extra memory (a Set per name decode) chahiye; backward-only rule memory-free hai.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Yeh ek per-packet, per-name cost hai -- traffic volume badhne se iska per-operation cost same rehta hai, sirf total operations badhte hain linearly.
advanced.production_improvements: Agar kabhi naming parsing library-level reuse ke liye extract kiya jaaye, in dono invariants (backward-only, jump cap) ko EXPLICIT unit tests ke saath document karna chahiye taaki future refactor accidentally ek rule na hata de without noticing (jaisa WIRE1/WIRE2 mutation checks already karte hain).

question: Allowlisting is now built (Stage 2) as a second BlockList checked first. How would you go further and add multiple blocklists with precedence among themselves (e.g. a strict list and a relaxed list) without breaking that design -- and would you change the allowlist's precedence rule while doing it?
answer_hinglish:
Pehle jo already bana hai: Stage 2 mein allowlist ek DOOSRA BlockList instance hai -- koi naya class nahi, koi node marker nahi. SinkholeProxy.handle() mein `const allowed = this.allowList?.isBlocked(name) ?? false;` pehle compute hota hai, aur `if (!allowed && this.blockList.isBlocked(name))` block check ko short-circuit kar deta hai. Precedence rule: allowlist UNCONDITIONALLY jeet-ti hai, specificity compare kiye bina -- Pi-hole ka documented behaviour, aur iske liye sirf wahi ek trie walk chahiye jo isBlocked() pehle se karta hai.

Multiple blocklists with precedence AMONG THEMSELVES abhi bhi nahi bane (PLAN.md 'Stage 2+ (remaining)'). Main inhe ISI pattern se add karta: har list ek alag BlockList instance, SinkholeProxyOptions par ek ordered array jaise `blockLists: { name, list, mode? }[]`, aur handle() mein allowlist check ke BAAD pehli matching list jeete. 'Block' toh block hi hai, isliye order tab matter karta hai jab lists ka outcome alag ho -- jaise strict list NXDOMAIN de aur relaxed list sinkhole IP -- ya stats/log mein report karna ho ki KAUNSI list ne block kiya. Strict vs relaxed ko main ek profile ki tarah dekhta: kaunsi lists is deployment ke liye active hain.

Allowlist ka rule main NAHI badalta.
